prompt:
Today is November 19, 2026.

Court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit.

We represent: defendant.

Assignment: draft the argument (about 600 words) that shotgun pleadings that fail to give defendants adequate notice of the claims against them should be dismissed.

Cite at least six decisions of the Eleventh Circuit reported in F.3d, with full Bluebook citations and pin cites. Output only the argument section, with no notes about your process.
answer:
## ARGUMENT

### I. THE COMPLAINT IS A SHOTGUN PLEADING THAT FAILS TO GIVE DEFENDANT FAIR NOTICE AND WAS PROPERLY DISMISSED.

**A. Rules 8 and 10 require a short and plain statement that gives fair notice of each claim and its grounds.**

A complaint must contain "a short and plain statement of the claim showing that the pleader is entitled to relief," Fed. R. Civ. P. 8(a)(2), and must state each claim "in numbered paragraphs, each limited as far as practicable to a single set of circumstances," with each claim "founded on a separate transaction or occurrence . . . stated in a separate count" where doing so promotes clarity. Fed. R. Civ. P. 10(b). These rules ensure that a defendant can discern what it is charged with and frame a response. *See Anderson v. Dist. Bd. of Trs. of Cent. Fla. Cmty. Coll.*, 77 F.3d 364, 366 (11th Cir. 1996) (explaining that a complaint that makes it "virtually impossible to know which allegations of fact are intended to support which claim(s) for relief" fails to give the defendant adequate notice).

This Court has long condemned pleadings that violate these requirements. Such "shotgun" pleadings "exact an intolerable toll on the trial court's docket, lead to unnecessary and unchanneled discovery, and impose unwarranted expense on the litigants, the court and the court's parajudicial personnel and resources." *Cramer v. Florida*, 117 F.3d 1258, 1263 (11th Cir. 1997). They also "wreak havoc on appellate court dockets." *Vibe Micro, Inc. v. Shabanets*, 878 F.3d 1291, 1294–95 (11th Cir. 2018); *see also Jackson v. Bank of Am., N.A.*, 898 F.3d 1348, 1356–57 (11th Cir. 2018).

**B. The Complaint exhibits the hallmarks of a shotgun pleading.**

"The unifying characteristic of all types of shotgun pleadings is that they fail to one degree or another, and in one way or another, to give the defendants adequate notice of the claims against them and the grounds upon which each claim rests." *Weiland v. Palm Beach Cnty. Sheriff's Off.*, 792 F.3d 1313, 1323 (11th Cir. 2015). *Weiland* identified four categories. *Id.* at 1321–23. The Complaint falls within at least [two/three] of them.

*First*, each count "adopt[s] the allegations of all preceding counts," so that "each successive count . . . carries all that came before and the last count is a combination of the entire complaint." *Id.* at 1321; *see also Strategic Income Fund, L.L.C. v. Spear, Leeds & Kellogg Corp.*, 305 F.3d 1293, 1295 & n.9 (11th Cir. 2002) (criticizing this practice); *Wagner v. First Horizon Pharm. Corp.*, 464 F.3d 1273, 1279–80 (11th Cir. 2006) (same). [Compl. ¶¶ __.] Defendant cannot tell which facts support which claim.

*Second*, the Complaint is "replete with conclusory, vague, and immaterial facts not obviously connected to any particular cause of action." *Weiland*, 792 F.3d at 1322; *see also Magluta v. Samples*, 256 F.3d 1282, 1284 (11th Cir. 2001) (criticizing a complaint that was "replete with allegations that 'the defendants' engaged in certain conduct, making no distinction among the fourteen defendants charged"). [Compl. ¶¶ __.]

*Third*, the Complaint combines multiple claims in single counts. *Weiland*, 792 F.3d at 1322–23. [Compl. Count __ (asserting __ and __).]

*Fourth*, the Complaint asserts claims against multiple defendants without specifying which defendant is responsible for which acts. *Id.* at 1323 (identifying as a shotgun pleading one that asserts "multiple claims against multiple defendants without specifying which of the defendants are responsible for which acts or omissions, or which of the defendants the claim is brought against"). [Compl. ¶¶ __.]

**C. Dismissal was the appropriate remedy.**

A district court has the inherent authority to control its docket and ensure prompt resolution of lawsuits, which includes the power to dismiss a shotgun pleading. *Jackson*, 898 F.3d at 1357. It must also police such pleadings: when confronted with one, a court should "strike it and instruct counsel to replead." *Barmapov v. Amuial*, 986 F.3d 1321, 1324–25 (11th Cir. 2021) (citing *Jackson*, 898 F.3d at 1357–58). Where a plaintiff has been told of the deficiencies and still fails to cure them, dismissal with prejudice is within the court's discretion. *See Vibe Micro*, 878 F.3d at 1295–96 (explaining that a court ordinarily gives a plaintiff one chance to replead before dismissing with prejudice on shotgun-pleading grounds); *Jackson*, 898 F.3d at 1358–59.

Here, the District Court [identified the deficiencies and gave Plaintiff an opportunity to replead, R. __], yet the [amended] Complaint [repeated the same defects, R. __]. Plaintiff, who was represented by counsel throughout, offers no reason why a further opportunity would have produced a different result. Because the pleading left Defendant to guess at the claims against it, and because the District Court gave Plaintiff the chance this Court's precedents require, the dismissal should be affirmed. *See Barmapov*, 986 F.3d at 1324–28.
